name: Locus coeruleus
summary: The locus coeruleus is a compact column of pigmented noradrenergic neurons in the upper pontine tegmentum beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, at the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray, whose axons reach almost the entire brain and spinal cord. With only a few tens of thousands of cells it supplies most of the noradrenaline of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum and thalamus and is the engine of arousal, vigilance and the response to novelty and stress. It regulates the sleep–wake cycle, is silent in REM sleep, and modulates pain in the spinal dorsal horn. It degenerates early in Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease, contributing to the sleep, autonomic and cognitive symptoms that precede the classical signs, and it is the site of the neuromelanin signal that can now be imaged.

anatomy.location: Dorsolateral tegmentum of the rostral pons beneath the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle, medial to the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus and lateral to the periaqueductal gray, extending into the caudal midbrain; its blue-black pigment is visible to the naked eye on a cut brainstem.

afferents.from: Nucleus paragigantocellularis and the nucleus of the solitary tract

efferents.to: Entire cerebral cortex, hippocampus and thalamus
Spinal dorsal horn and intermediolateral column

function: Locus coeruleus neurons fire tonically during waking, phasically to salient stimuli and fall silent in REM sleep; their noradrenaline release through beta and alpha receptors increases the signal-to-noise ratio of cortical processing, focuses attention, promotes memory consolidation in the hippocampus and amygdala, and drives the sympathetic response to stress through the hypothalamus and the medullary pressor centers. Descending fibers to the dorsal horn inhibit pain transmission, and cerebellar fibers modulate Purkinje cell excitability. The nucleus is inhibited by opioids and clonidine and activated by their withdrawal, which produces the sweating, anxiety and tachycardia of the withdrawal syndrome.

bestView.label: dorsolateral rostral pontine tegmentum beneath the fourth ventricle
rostral pons at the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: A few millimeters of tissue in the dorsolateral pontine tegmentum, not seen on routine sequences; neuromelanin-sensitive T1 imaging shows it as a small bright focus on each side of the fourth ventricle at the level of the rostral pons.

pathology.pathology: Parkinson disease and Lewy body disease
pathology.finding: Loss of the neuromelanin signal of the locus coeruleus on neuromelanin-sensitive imaging, often before nigral loss, correlating with REM sleep behavior disorder.
Infarct, demyelination or Wernicke encephalopathy involving the periaqueductal and dorsal pontine tegmentum with hypersomnolence.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the noradrenergic drive to the cortex and thalamus

lesionEffects.deficit: REM sleep behavior disorder and autonomic dysfunction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Early Lewy body degeneration of the coeruleus and neighboring nuclei
Loss of noradrenergic modulation of prefrontal and hippocampal circuits in Alzheimer disease

examination: Attention testing (digit span, vigilance) in neurodegenerative disease
pearls: Opioid withdrawal is a locus coeruleus storm, which is why clonidine, which silences the nucleus, relieves it
The coeruleus is one of the first nuclei to degenerate in Parkinson and Alzheimer disease, decades before diagnosis
It is silent in REM sleep; its early loss is linked to REM sleep behavior disorder

pitfalls: Isolated lesions of the locus coeruleus are not clinically recognized; its disorders are pharmacological and degenerative
